prompt: Write a spoken word piece from the perspective of a junior safety researcher watching her VP prepare for the annual audit. She's describing what she sees: the strongest results moved to the front, the most rigorous-sounding methods highlighted, the mixed and inconclusive findings reframed as active research, the level of detail carefully tuned so the non-technical committee won't ask hard questions. She's not accusing him of lying — she's describing the architecture of selective truth. Make the curation strategies specific and precise within the poem.
response:
# The Arrangement

She watches him build it —
not a lie, never a lie,
something more careful than that.

---

He opens with the adversarial robustness numbers,
the ones from the February red-team,
the model that was *already patched* before the team even ran the suite,
so the pass rate sits at ninety-four percent
and he puts it on slide three,
which is where the eye lands
when the committee is still paying attention,
still holding their coffee with both hands,
still performing the posture of diligence.

He does not mention the March red-team.
He does not *hide* the March red-team.
If you asked him, he would say
*it's in the appendix,*
and it is,
page forty-seven,
in a table with no caption
and a footnote that reads
*"methodology under revision,"*
which is true
the way a locked door is *ajar*
because somewhere in the building
someone has a key.

---

I watch him choose the word *"promising."*

The alignment tax study showed
a three-percent capability drop
when the safety filter was active
and a fourteen-percent drop
on the tasks that actually matter —
the agentic ones, the multi-step reasoning,
the ones the product team has staked the quarter on —
but three percent is the number
that goes on the slide,
averaged across all benchmarks
like you'd average a hospital:
*the patients are, on balance, alive.*

*"Promising,"* he types.
*"Within acceptable bounds."*

He does not define the bounds.
The committee will not ask.
The committee has never once
asked who set the bounds.

---

The hallucination study is the one
that keeps me up.

We ran four evaluation protocols.
Two showed improvement.
One showed regression.
One was — I'll use the word — *ambiguous,*
which in our field means
*we argued for three weeks
and nobody changed their mind.*

He takes the two that showed improvement,
puts them under the header **Results.**
He takes the regression,
puts it under the header **Ongoing Work.**
He takes the ambiguous one
and puts it under **Future Directions,**
which is the place where findings go
to be *respected*
and *never seen again.*

Same data. Four quadrants of the same study.
But now they live in different houses
and the committee will read them
as four different stories:
success, success, effort, ambition.

---

He adjusts the technical depth
the way you'd season food
for someone else's palate.

The RLHF pipeline description
loses its paragraph on reward hacking.
Not deleted — *condensed*
into the phrase *"iterative refinement,"*
which is accurate
the way *"renovation"* is accurate
for a building that caught fire.

The capability evaluations keep their specifics:
*parameter counts, benchmark names, percentage gains.*
The safety evaluations get *"qualitative assessment"*
and *"expert review,"*
which means me,
which means the afternoon I spent
writing a report he summarized
into a single bullet point
that says *"no critical issues identified,"*
which is not what I wrote.
What I wrote was
*"no critical issues identified*
***under the conditions tested,***
*which do not yet include—"*

But the sentence ends where his summary begins.

---

He's not a villain. That's the thing
I need you to understand.

He held the door for me this morning.
He fought for our headcount in Q3.
He believes — I think he genuinely believes —
that the work is good,
that the model is safe *enough,*
that the committee doesn't need
the full topology of our uncertainty
because uncertainty
is not a thing that survives
a boardroom.

He is building an *architecture.*
Load-bearing walls of real results.
Decorative facades of context removal.
The weight distributed so carefully
that the structure stands
as long as nobody
walks through every room.

---

The audit will take forty minutes.
There will be seven slides.
There will be two questions,
both about timeline,
none about methodology.
The committee will approve continued deployment
and someone will say the word *"robust"*
and someone will say *"encouraged"*
and the minutes will reflect
that safety was *discussed*
and *addressed*
and I will be thanked by name
in the acknowledgments section
of a document
that contains my work
the way a river contains
the rain —

*completely,*
*unrecognizably,*
*and only in the direction*
*it was already flowing.*

---

He sends me the deck at 4 PM.
Subject line: *"Final version — thanks for all your help."*

I open it.
I read it.
Everything in it is true.

That is the problem.
Everything in it is *true.*
